Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally during the first year after birth.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the medical team that’s directly caring for you; it won’t go anywhere else without your permission. My goal is to create a comfortable, judgment-free space so you can answer as honestly as possible—there are no right or wrong replies.  

We’ll go through one question at a time, focusing on how you’ve felt over the past seven days. If any question feels difficult, just let me know and we can slow down or pause. Ready to begin?  

First, I’d like to know:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

Honestly, it’s been hard. I used to laugh all the time—my husband would make a dumb joke and I’d crack up—but this week, even when he tries, it just feels… flat. I might smile for a second, but it fades fast, like I’m too tired or heavy to really enjoy it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… nothing’s felt funny lately.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try, but most of the time it feels like I’m just going through the motions. There are a couple of things I still want to do—like when my sister said she’d bring coffee tomorrow, I felt a tiny spark—but it’s way less than before. Everything else feels kind of gray.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours, and I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or that I’m just not soothing him right. I know, rationally, babies cry, but the guilt still sits there. It’s not every second, but it pops up most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly picture him choking, or I’ll hear a siren and imagine accidents that haven’t happened. I can usually talk myself down, but the thoughts keep circling back, especially at night when I’m trying to sleep.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even if everything looks fine. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get the baby down and see the sink full of bottles or the laundry mountain, and it’s like my chest tightens. Some mornings I just sit on the couch staring at it all, wondering how I’ll get through the next hour, but I still manage—no pills or wine, just gritting my teeth and pushing on.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—worrying the baby will stop breathing, replaying everything I think I did wrong that day. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I wake up with a jolt a couple of times a night, heart racing, sure I heard him cry.
I have felt sad or miserable
Most of the week, really. It’s like a gray cloud that settles in the morning and just lingers. I’ll look at the baby and feel flashes of love, but underneath there’s this heavy sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times. Once was after I finally got him to nap and I sat down to pump—my back ached, the kitchen was a mess, and I just felt like I was failing. I ended up sobbing into a dish towel so no one would hear.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s crossed my mind once or twice this week, just a quick flash—like “what if I weren’t here?”—but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to die. I push the thought away because I know I need to be here for my baby, but it still scared me that it popped up at all.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly gray and heavy. Humor that once came easily now feels distant, and even small sparks of excitement are rare. Each day brings waves of worry about your baby's safety, sudden panicky surges, and a sense that the simplest tasks are piling up beyond what you can manage. Nights are long, filled with racing thoughts and repeated awakenings, while mornings bring a persistent sad cloud that lingers no matter how much you love your little one. You've also been startled by fleeting thoughts of not being here, though you emphatically want to stay and care for your child.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete loss of ability to see humor, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced anticipatory enjoyment—"way less than before" and "gray"—but still experiences occasional sparks, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame ('pops up most days'), aligning with 'some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily intrusive worry images ('pretty much every day', 'keep circling back') matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>The patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring multiple times in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, chest-tightening anxiety, and difficulty facing basic tasks, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep disruption with racing thoughts and repeated awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness lingering most days, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "a couple of times" triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring yields 24/30, well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. The patient endorses core <sym>depressive symptoms</sym>: pervasive sadness, loss of interest, daily crying, and self-blame, alongside prominent <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym>. <sym>Insomnia</sym> is mood-related, and <sym>self-harm ideation</sym> (Q10 score 1) mandates immediate safety assessment. DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> are met by >/= 5 symptoms present most days for >/= 2 weeks causing impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Identify support people who can stay with you tonight and help with baby care while you seek treatment
4. Begin basic self-care: accept help with chores, aim for brief outdoor walks, eat small regular snacks, and use 5-minute breathing breaks when panic surges
5. Discuss tonight with a professional whether short-term medication or therapy referrals are appropriate; bring this EPDS summary to your appointment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
